passages.text: For years, delivery by drone seemed to be a technology that was always just around the corner. Recently it has finally begun to materialize, at least in a handful of locales. In parts of the Dallas area, you can order household staples from a large retailer, and a small drone then lowers them into your yard, often within half an hour. The company Zipline has been flying blood and other medical supplies to hospitals in Rwanda since 2016, and it has since extended its service to several other countries. Proponents argue that drones can reach outlying clinics faster than trucks on rutted roads; for lightweight parcels, they add, drones also use far less energy than a delivery van. Regulation has been the most formidable impediment. Most rules have required that each drone stay within sight of a human operator, which renders long routes impractical and keeps costs high. In the United States, the Federal Aviation Administration has granted case-by-case exemptions for some companies to fly beyond that limit, and in 2025 it proposed rules intended to make such flights commonplace. ____, technical approval does not guarantee public acceptance. In some neighborhoods, residents have grumbled about the incessant buzzing overhead; others fret about privacy, since many drones carry cameras. The economics also remain precarious. Each flight can carry only a small parcel, and inclement weather can ground an entire fleet. For now, drone delivery looks less like a substitute for trucks than a useful supplement in particular niches.

In May 2024, a Singapore Airlines flight from London to Singapore encountered severe turbulence over Myanmar. The aircraft plunged abruptly, passengers who were not strapped in were catapulted against the ceiling, and one elderly passenger died, apparently of cardiac arrest. The plane diverted to Bangkok, and dozens of people were treated in hospital there. The mishap drew attention to a question that atmospheric scientists had been probing for years: is turbulence becoming more common as the climate warms? Much of the most hazardous turbulence is of the clear-air kind, which occurs without visible clouds; the weather radar that pilots use cannot detect it. It is generated largely by wind shear, the difference in wind speed between neighboring layers of air, and shear is most pronounced around the jet streams. Accumulating greenhouse gases alter the temperature differences at the altitudes where airliners cruise, and this appears to be intensifying the shear inside the jet streams. A 2023 study by researchers at the University of Reading, which used data from 1979 to 2020, found that the total yearly duration of severe clear-air turbulence at a typical point over the North Atlantic had swelled by about 55 percent. So should you be worried the next time you fly? Modern airliners are engineered to withstand forces far greater than turbulence normally produces, so the peril to the aircraft itself is slight. The real risk falls on people inside the cabin who are ____. Airlines are therefore investing in more accurate forecasts and exhorting passengers to keep their seat belts fastened whenever they are seated.

Empathy, the capacity to share and respond to the distress of others, was long thought to be largely confined to humans and perhaps a few other primates. A series of experiments at the University of Chicago, published in 2011, challenged that view. The subject was an unprepossessing one: the laboratory rat. In each trial, one rat roamed freely in an arena while a cagemate was trapped inside a cramped transparent tube, which could be opened only from the outside, by nudging a door with some exertion. At first the free rats seemed perturbed, circling the tube and gnawing at its walls. Within days, the majority had learned to open the door and liberate their companions, and they did so swiftly and deliberately. When the tube was empty or contained a toy rat, by contrast, the free rats seldom bothered to open it. Then the researchers gave the rats a thornier dilemma: a second tube was filled with chocolate chips, a delicacy rats prize highly. Instead of devouring the whole treat themselves, many free rats opened both tubes and left part of the chocolate for the freed companion. The researchers were careful to emphasize that rats do not experience the world as people do. Still, the results suggest that the behavior was driven by something like ____ rather than by curiosity or the prospect of a reward. After all, releasing the cagemate brought the free rat nothing it could eat or use.

Economists have long recognized that many workers save too little for retirement. Simply admonishing them to save more seldom works. In the late 1990s, the economists Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi designed a program that took an unorthodox approach: rather than combating the habits of mind that thwart saving, it tried to harness them. They called it "Save More Tomorrow," and it rested on three insights about human behavior. First, people find it far easier to commit to a sacrifice in the future than to make one today. Isn't it easier to promise a diet next month than to forgo dessert tonight? Second, people loathe seeing their take-home pay dwindle, even by a small amount. Third, once people are enrolled in a plan, most of them stay in it, because changing anything takes effort. Traditional retirement plans, the economists noticed, asked workers to defy all three tendencies at once. You had to curtail your spending immediately, accept a smaller paycheck, and make an active decision. Employees were therefore invited to commit, in advance, to setting aside a portion of each future pay raise, so their take-home pay never shrank. They could withdraw from the program at any time, but few did. At the first company to pilot it, participants' average savings rate rose from about 3.5 percent of their pay to more than 13 percent within a few years. Since then, the idea has ____. In the United States, a 2006 statute encouraged employers to enroll workers automatically in plans that raise contributions step by step, and employers in many other countries have since adopted similar designs.

In the early 1950s the de Havilland Comet, the world's first jet airliner, was the pride of British aviation. Then, in 1954, two Comets disintegrated in the air within a few months, and investigators struggled to ascertain why. There were no survivors and no record of what had happened in the cockpit. Among the scientists asked to help was David Warren, a young researcher at a government aeronautical laboratory in Melbourne, Australia. Warren had an idea that seemed self-evident once it was articulated. What if a small device on board could record the pilots' voices and the readings of the main instruments? Investigators would then know far more about the final minutes of a flight. Until then, they had to rely on scattered shards of metal and on the accounts of witnesses on the ground, neither of which could reveal what the crew had seen, said, or tried to do at the end. Warren had recently seen a miniature recorder at a trade fair and realized that such machines could be adapted for the purpose. By the late 1950s he and his colleagues had built a working prototype, which stored several hours of sound and data on a thin steel wire. The reaction at home was disheartening. Aviation officials saw little merit in the device. Pilots objected to having their conversations recorded, fearing that the machine would be used for covert surveillance. Would you want every word you said at work kept on tape? The idea found a more receptive audience in Britain, where officials could see its value for investigating accidents. Attitudes in Australia shifted after a fatal crash in 1960 that investigators could not fully explain, and the country soon became one of the first to mandate flight recorders on its airliners. Today every large passenger plane carries them, and they are popularly known as "black boxes." In fact, they are painted ____ so that searchers can spot them among the wreckage. They are built to survive searing heat, crushing impact, and prolonged immersion in the sea. The information they preserve has helped to elucidate countless accidents and to prevent many more.

For decades, most aid to impoverished households took the form of goods and services chosen by outsiders: livestock, sewing machines, training courses, or bags of grain. The rationale seemed sound. Donors were apprehensive that if they simply handed over money, it might be squandered on alcohol and tobacco rather than on food and school fees. Giving goods also allowed donors to trace exactly how their money had been used. (A) In the last twenty years, however, a growing body of evidence has undermined that assumption. Much of it stems from Kenya, where mobile-phone money transfers became ubiquitous in the late 2000s. (B) A charity called GiveDirectly, founded by a group of young economists, began disbursing sums of cash directly to poor households in rural villages, with no conditions attached. Researchers then compared households that received transfers with similar households that did not. The households that received money were chosen at random, so differences between the two groups could reasonably be attributed to the cash itself. A widely cited study published in 2016 found that recipients increased their spending on food, invested in durable assets such as metal roofs and livestock, and reported less anxiety and greater life satisfaction. Economists at the World Bank reviewed studies from many countries and reached a similar conclusion: on average, cash transfers did not increase spending on alcohol or tobacco, and in many cases such spending fell. (C) Advocates of cash aid draw a broader lesson from such findings. People living in poverty, they argue, generally understand their own needs better than distant planners do. A farmer may need a new roof more than a goat, and a mother may need school fees more than a sewing machine. Treating recipients as capable decision makers, they add, also preserves a sense of dignity that handouts of goods can undermine. ____, it is often cheaper to deliver money through a phone than to buy, ship, and distribute goods. Cash also lets families cope with emergencies, such as an illness or a failed harvest, that no planner could have anticipated. (D) Skeptics raise legitimate concerns: some worry that large transfers could inflate local prices and penalize neighbors who receive nothing. Others ask a simple question: "What happens once the money is spent?" Some economists also point out that cash cannot build roads or hospitals; those still require public investment. Researchers are now conducting long-term experiments to answer such questions. Even so, the burden of proof has shifted. Many aid agencies now compare their programs against the simple benchmark of handing people cash.

For most of the space age, rockets were used once and discarded. After lifting its payload toward orbit, a booster would plummet into the ocean or burn up in the atmosphere, and the next launch required a brand-new one. Critics of the practice liked to ask, "Would you fly with an airline that scrapped each jet after a single trip?" That has begun to change. In December 2015, the company SpaceX landed the first stage of a Falcon 9 rocket upright on a landing pad after sending satellites into orbit, and within two years it was flying salvaged boosters again; some individual boosters have since flown more than twenty missions. In October 2024, the company went further, catching the colossal first stage of its Starship rocket in mid-air with a pair of mechanical arms on the launch tower. Rival companies and space agencies, in the United States, China, and elsewhere, are now developing reusable rockets of their own. The chief allure is cost. Building a booster accounts for a hefty share of the price of a launch. Reusing it allows that outlay to be amortized across many flights. ____, launching a satellite has become considerably cheaper, and the objects sent into orbit have proliferated. Reuse is not costless, however. Recovered boosters must be scrutinized and refurbished, and a rocket that carries fuel for landing can carry less to orbit. Engineers contend that these costs are worth bearing. How far reuse can lower prices, though, will hinge on how quickly a booster can be turned around.

When air travel imploded in 2020, airlines around the world parked their planes and encouraged thousands of experienced pilots to retire early. Few foresaw that within two or three years they would be scrambling to find enough people to fly and fix their aircraft. So what went wrong? As demand for travel rebounded, the industry discovered that the personnel it had let go could not be swiftly replaced. Part of the predicament is time and money. Becoming an airline pilot entails hundreds of hours of flight training. In many countries, students must shell out tens of thousands of dollars for it before earning a single paycheck. In the United States, rules adopted after a fatal regional airline crash in 2009 require most new first officers to have logged 1,500 hours of flight time. Meeting that requirement alone is a laborious process. At the other end of a career, American airline pilots must retire at 65. A large generation of pilots hired in the 1980s and 1990s is now reaching that age. Maintenance faces a comparable squeeze, since many veteran mechanics are nearing retirement and too few young technicians are entering the profession. The shortages have had tangible effects: some smaller airlines have axed routes to towns that were already poorly served. ____, airlines have raised wages, opened their own flight academies, and offered to defray training costs for promising students. Such measures will take years to bear fruit, because no amount of money can shorten the time it takes to train a safe pilot or a skilled mechanic.

A dung beetle that has sculpted a ball of dung faces an urgent problem: rival beetles are eager to steal it. Its best strategy is to roll the ball away from the crowded dung pile in a straight line. A straight path carries it away from competitors most efficiently. Researchers in South Africa noticed that beetles manage this feat even on moonless nights, and they set out to discover how. In experiments published in 2013, the scientists fitted some beetles with tiny cardboard caps that blocked their view of the sky. Capped beetles wandered erratically. Those with an unobstructed view rolled their balls along remarkably straight routes. To identify which celestial cues mattered, the team moved the experiments into a planetarium in Johannesburg, where they could display or conceal particular features of the night sky, something real nights never permit. When only the brightest individual stars were shown, the beetles' performance deteriorated, but when only the diffuse glow of the Milky Way was visible, they oriented almost as well as under a full starry sky. The insects' compound eyes are probably too ____ to distinguish most individual stars. They can, however, detect the luminous band of the galaxy and keep it at a constant angle. The finding made the dung beetle the first animal known to navigate by the Milky Way. It is a reminder that sophisticated orientation does not require a large brain.

Few habits are extolled as consistently as thrift. Parents exhort their children to save, and households that put money aside for hard times are rightly deemed prudent. If you have ever cut back on spending because a recession seemed imminent, you were doing exactly what sensible people do. Yet economists have long observed that what is wise for one family can become ____ when everyone does it at once. The idea is known as the "paradox of thrift." Versions of the argument appeared as early as the eighteenth century, but it is most closely identified with the British economist John Maynard Keynes, who developed it during the Great Depression of the 1930s. The reasoning runs as follows. In an economy, one person's expenditure is another person's income. When a single household retrenches, the effect on the wider economy is negligible, and the family ends up with more savings. But suppose that, dreading a recession, millions of households cut their spending at the same time. Shops sell less, factories scale back production, and workers lose hours or jobs. Because incomes slump, people find that they cannot save as much as they had planned, and some must deplete the savings they already have. In the end, the collective endeavor to save more may leave the total amount of saving unchanged or even lower, while the economy shrinks. This logic helps explain why many governments try to increase their own spending during severe downturns, even as households tighten their belts. Critics retort that such spending must eventually be repaid and that government debt carries risks of its own. The debate over how much the state should spend in a crisis has never been resolved, but few economists now repudiate the paradox itself.

In the mid-1990s, the social psychologists Claude Steele and Joshua Aronson ran a simple experiment that later grew into one of the most debated studies in their field. Black and white undergraduates at an elite American university took an arduous test made up of questions from a graduate school entrance exam. For some students, the test was described as a measure of intellectual ability. For others, it was framed as a laboratory exercise about problem solving that said nothing about ability. When the test was billed as a measure of ability, Black students scored conspicuously lower than white students with similar academic records. When it was not, the gap largely vanished. Why would a mere label change the scores? Steele and Aronson called the phenomenon stereotype threat: when people know that a negative stereotype exists about their group, the fear of confirming it can breed anxiety, divert attention, and sap the mental resources needed for difficult tasks. The idea was soon extended to other groups; studies reported, for example, that women performed worse on challenging math tests when reminded of the stereotype that men are better at mathematics. The effect even seemed to surface among groups not usually seen as disadvantaged, such as white men, who in one study did worse on a hard math test when told that their scores would be compared with those of Asian students. The research had an encouraging implication: if part of a performance gap was created by the testing situation, then changing the situation might shrink it. Schools experimented with brief interventions, such as having students write about values that mattered to them. In one widely reported case, a short writing exercise given to middle school students early in the year was said to narrow the achievement gap over the following months. In recent years, however, the field has confronted thornier questions. Some large studies designed to replicate the original findings have produced smaller effects than expected, or none at all, and researchers have also debated whether early results were inflated by small samples. Few psychologists now maintain that stereotype threat explains most differences in test scores. Many still think it is real in some situations, but the effect appears to be ____ than was once believed.

For twenty-seven years, a small number of affluent travelers could cross the Atlantic in about three and a half hours. The Concorde, built jointly by Britain and France, entered passenger service in 1976 and cruised at more than twice the speed of sound. Yet despite all its speed and glamour, it never became the future of air travel that its designers had imagined. Only twenty were ever manufactured, and British Airways and Air France retired their fleets in 2003. Passengers paid many times the price of an ordinary ticket, and the aircraft became a symbol of luxury and national pride. (A) So why did it fail? Its fuel consumption was prodigious, its fares were exorbitant for ordinary travelers, and a fatal crash near Paris in 2000 eroded public confidence. The most fundamental constraint, however, was noise. An aircraft flying faster than sound produces shock waves that reach the ground as a sonic boom. If you lived beneath the flight path, you would hear an abrupt thunderclap that could rattle windows for miles. (B) In 1973, the United States banned civilian aircraft from flying faster than sound over land, and other countries imposed similar restrictions. These confined the Concorde largely to routes over the ocean, which ____. Engineers have spent decades seeking a feasible way to circumvent the problem. The key insight is that the contour of an aircraft dictates how its shock waves coalesce. A long, carefully sculpted nose and fuselage can keep the waves from merging into a single powerful boom, so that people on the ground hear only a soft thump. The idea is not new, but only in recent decades have computer simulations made it possible to design such shapes with confidence. (C) NASA has built an experimental jet called the X-59 to test the idea; unveiled in January 2024, the aircraft has a nose so elongated that the pilot cannot see straight ahead and must rely on a camera and a screen instead. The X-59 is not intended to carry passengers. Its purpose is to fly over designated communities and gauge how residents react to the quieter sound. The results will be shared with regulators, who must decide whether the overland ban could be replaced by a noise limit. (D) Several private companies are already designing supersonic airliners in the hope that regulators will lift the ban.

On May 27, 2024, South Korea opened a new national space agency, the Korea AeroSpace Administration, in Sacheon in South Gyeongsang Province. Its establishment marked a watershed in the way the country runs its space program. Until then, responsibility for space policy had been fragmented among several government bodies. Officials argued that this disjointed structure, in which research institutes reported to a science ministry that also oversaw many unrelated fields, hampered large, long-term projects and impeded swift responses to a rapidly evolving industry. The new agency consolidated policy, research, and industrial support under a single roof. Major institutes were placed under its direction, including the Korea Aerospace Research Institute, the developer of the country's Nuri rocket. Nuri had already shown what Korean engineers could accomplish. It placed satellites into orbit in 2022 and 2023, and the lunar orbiter Danuri had been circling the Moon since December 2022. The government has set lofty goals for the agency, including a Moon landing in the early 2030s and a much larger domestic space industry. Attaining them will be arduous: Korea's space budget remains modest next to those of the United States, China, or Japan. The agency must also vie with established players for talent and contracts. Even its location has been contentious, since many researchers are based far away in Daejeon. So why bother with a new agency at all? ____, supporters argue that a dedicated agency gives Korea something it lacked before: a clear voice for space in government and a single partner for international cooperation.

If you live near a busy airport, the roar of jet engines is not an occasional nuisance but a perpetual feature of daily life. At peak hours, aircraft may pass overhead every minute or two. They drown out conversations and disrupt classes, and near airports that operate at night, they break sleep. A typical resident might shrug and say, "You stop hearing it after a while." The body, research suggests, does not. Studies in several countries have linked long-term exposure to aircraft noise with disturbed sleep, higher blood pressure, and an increased risk of heart disease. Disentangling the effects of noise from those of income and air pollution, however, is difficult. Some studies have also found that children at schools under flight paths lag behind in reading. In 2018, the World Health Organization recommended a stricter limit for aircraft noise than for road traffic noise, citing its particularly intrusive character. Governments have attempted several remedies: some airports, including Gimpo in Seoul, close to most flights late at night, and others charge higher landing fees for noisier planes. Many subsidize double-glazed windows and better insulation in nearby homes and schools. Newer aircraft are also considerably quieter than those of a few decades ago. Yet these gains are frequently offset by growth in air traffic, so that ____. Residents who feel ignored increasingly mobilize to oppose new runways, turning airport noise into a political issue as much as a technical one.

Do spiders dream? The question sounds whimsical, but it touches a serious scientific puzzle. Rapid eye movement sleep, the stage most closely tied to vivid dreams in humans, was long studied almost exclusively in mammals and birds. Detecting it in other animals is daunting, since researchers usually rely on recordings of brain activity, or on watching the eyes flicker beneath closed lids. Jumping spiders, however, offered an unexpected window: these diminutive hunters have large, forward-facing eyes. In newly hatched spiders, the body is so ____ that you can see the long tubes behind the eyes from the outside; the animals move these tubes to shift their gaze. In a study published in 2022, researchers in Germany filmed young jumping spiders at night as they dangled inert from silk threads. Every so often, the spiders' eye tubes began to flit back and forth in brief bursts, much as human eyes do during REM sleep. During these same episodes, their legs twitched and curled, and the bursts recurred at fairly regular intervals throughout the night. The researchers were careful not to claim that the spiders dream. Do these episodes serve the same purposes as REM sleep in mammals, such as consolidating memories? No one knows, and no one can ask a spider what it experiences, so answering that question will require ways of studying the inner life of animals that do not yet exist. Still, the observations raise the possibility that something like REM sleep evolved far earlier, or more often, than scientists had assumed.

Winning an auction feels like a coup, but economists warn that in certain auctions victory itself can be an ominous sign. The hazard arises when the item has roughly the same value to every bidder, but no one knows exactly what that value is. An oil field, for example, is worth whatever oil it contains, yet each company can only estimate that amount from its own surveys; some estimates will be too low, and others will be inflated. Now suppose every company bids according to its own estimate. Who wins? Usually the company with the most ____ estimate, which is likely to be too high. Unless bidders adjust for this, the winner tends to pay more than the item is worth. In 1971, engineers at an American oil company described the problem, arguing that firms bidding for offshore drilling rights in the Gulf of Mexico had reaped disappointingly low returns for precisely this reason. They called it the "winner's curse." You can see the effect in a classroom: ask students to bid on a jar of coins without telling them how much money it holds. The average bid is often below the true value, but the winning bid frequently exceeds it. Once again, the person who wins tends to be the one who has overestimated the most. The lesson for bidders is to pare their bids below their estimates and to pare them further as the number of rivals grows, since more bidders mean a higher chance that someone will overestimate. Sellers, meanwhile, have every incentive to foster crowded and zealous bidding. When several European governments auctioned licenses for mobile phone networks around 2000, companies paid exorbitant sums, and some later floundered under the debt they had taken on.

Imagine that you are locked inside a room and that you know no Chinese. Through a slot in the door come slips of paper covered in Chinese characters. You consult a massive rulebook, written in English, that tells you exactly what symbols to send back in response to each string you receive. The rules are so elaborate that your replies are flawless. To native speakers outside, the room appears to be holding a fluent conversation in Chinese. Yet you understand not a single word; you are merely matching shapes. This thought experiment, known as the Chinese room, was devised in 1980 by the American philosopher John Searle. His target was a claim popular among some researchers in artificial intelligence: that a computer running the right program would genuinely understand language and thus possess a mind. A computer, Searle observed, does exactly what the person in the room does: it manipulates symbols according to formal rules. If the person gains no understanding by following the rulebook, he argued, neither does the machine. In his famous formulation, syntax is not sufficient for semantics; shuffling symbols, in other words, is not the same as grasping meaning. The argument provoked a torrent of rebuttals. The most common, called the systems reply, concedes that the person does not understand Chinese. But doesn't the room as a whole, person and rulebook together, understand it? Searle retorted that the person could memorize the entire rulebook and work outside the room, and still understand nothing. Others contended that genuine understanding requires a body that perceives and acts in the world, so that symbols become linked to the things they stand for. For decades the debate seemed largely academic, since no existing program could converse convincingly. The arrival of chatbots capable of fluent, wide-ranging dialogue has revived it with unexpected urgency. Critics invoke Searle to argue that such systems merely predict plausible sequences of words. Defenders reply that the line between simulating understanding and possessing it may be harder to draw than the thought experiment suggests. Whichever side proves right, the Chinese room remains valuable because it ____.

Time-restricted eating is a form of intermittent fasting: you eat all your meals within a fixed window of, say, eight hours each day. It has become one of the most popular dietary fads of the past decade, and its allure is easy to fathom. Instead of counting calories, followers simply watch the clock, and many report feeling more in control of their eating. Supporters have also claimed benefits beyond weight loss, from better sleep to sharper concentration, though such claims are harder to test. Early enthusiasm owed much to animal studies. In a widely cited 2012 study, mice were fed a high-fat diet but allowed to eat only during an eight-hour window each day. They gained far less weight than mice that ate the same food whenever they liked, yet both groups consumed similar numbers of calories. Researchers proposed that eating in tune with the body's internal clock improved the way the animals processed fat and sugar. (A) Human trials have yielded a more nuanced picture. In a 2020 study, overweight adults who were told to eat only between noon and eight in the evening lost, over twelve weeks, little more weight than adults who ate on a normal schedule. They also lost a small amount of muscle, a finding that surprised the researchers. (B) A larger trial in China, published in 2022, followed two groups of people for a full year, both of which cut their calories, but only one of which also limited eating to an eight-hour window. ____, the time limit made no significant difference: both groups lost similar amounts of weight. These results suggest that, for many people, the benefits of time-restricted eating come mainly from eating less overall. (C) A shorter eating window may make it harder to snack late at night, for example. Skipping a late snack removes calories regardless of when the remaining meals are eaten. That is not a negligible advantage: a simple rule that people can adhere to may be more useful than an elaborate diet they abandon. But it also means that the clock itself may matter less than its champions claim. Researchers continue to study whether meal timing affects health in other ways, such as blood sugar control, and whether certain groups benefit more than others. (D) For now, most nutrition experts offer simple advice: the best diet is the one you can sustain.
